summary: A 1969 proposal for the software a time-sharing host should include to use the network. It suggests system-level primitives available to user programs and a subsystem called Telnet, which would let a terminal at a remote host act like a terminal at the serving host.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 15 proposes a Telnet program that lets someone at a terminal connect to a remote time-sharing host. It also describes commands for ending the session and transferring a file.

questions: network subsystem for time sharing hosts
what was the telnet subsystem proposal
subtitle: A proposal for terminal access to remote time-sharing hosts using Telnet.

tldr.problem: A user needed a direct way to reach a remote host from a terminal without writing a network program.
tldr.mechanism: The proposed Telnet subsystem uses the host's network primitives to connect a local terminal to a serving host and provides commands for connecting, logging out and copying files.
tldr.outcome: The author describes it as a simple level 0 network program that would soon be surpassed.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 15 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The author describes the proposed Telnet subsystem as a level 0 program that will quickly be surpassed.

sections.title: Network Primitives and Terminal Access
sections.content:
The note describes network primitives intended for host monitor systems: open a primary connection, open an auxiliary connection, transmit over a connection and close it. These system calls give user programs access to the network.

For direct terminal access, C. Stephen Carr proposes a subsystem called Telnet. It wraps the network primitives so a terminal at one host can function as a terminal at a serving host.
sections.plainLanguage: Host software provides basic operations for opening and using network connections. The proposed Telnet program uses those operations so a person can work with a remote host from a terminal.

sections.title: Telnet Commands and Connections
sections.content:
The user chooses an escape character. Text between that character and a carriage return goes to Telnet as a command instead of being sent to the serving host. The CONNECT TO command names the serving host; a successful connection places the user in a pre-logged-in state there.

LOGOUT asks the serving host to log out the user. COPY FILE transfers a file from the user's host to the serving host over an auxiliary connection. Telnet accepts its commands when first entered or after the escape character.
sections.plainLanguage: Most typing passes to the remote computer. The user can type an escape character to give a command to Telnet, such as connecting, logging out or copying a file.

sections.title: Example: A Utah User Connects to SRI
sections.content:
The example follows a user at Utah who wants to use the CAL subsystem on SRI's 940 computer. The user starts Telnet, chooses an escape character and connects to SRI. The connection succeeds only if SRI will accept another outside user and the Utah user is authorized for network access.

After logging in at SRI, the user's characters pass through to the serving host. The example also shows the user directing Telnet to send a local file over an auxiliary connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The example user connects from Utah to a computer at SRI and logs in there. The user can also ask Telnet to send a local file to the remote system.

sections.title: A Deliberately Simple First Program
sections.content: The author says that, with the network primitives, a Telnet subsystem at the user's host and a manual for the serving host, a remote user can use the network. The note calls Telnet a level 0 network program that will quickly be surpassed, while also saying it is simple enough to be working fairly soon.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal aims for a small, basic program that could make remote access useful soon. Its author expects more capable network programs to follow.
